 With two weeks until Election Day, early voting data reveals surprising differences in participation across political parties, states and demographic groups. A University of Florida researcher says Republican early voting is trailing previous midterms in North Carolina, while Black and Latino voters are showing significant increases in participation.
 Advertisement Updated: 3:12 PM PDT Oct 20, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ Christopher Salas White House Correspondent Marissa Mizroch Producer More than 13 million Americans have already voted. Here's what the early data reveals
 With two weeks until Election Day, early voting data reveals surprising differences in participation across political parties, states and demographic groups. A University of Florida researcher says Republican early voting is trailing previous midterms in North Carolina, while Black and Latino voters are showing significant increases in participation.
 Updated: 3:12 PM PDT Oct 20, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ Christopher Salas White House Correspondent Marissa Mizroch Producer WASHINGTON — More than 13 million Americans have already cast their ballots in the upcoming midterm elections, according to the University of Florida Election Lab, with early voting data revealing notable differences in participation across political parties, states and demographic groups.
 "We're just looking at probably a high turnout election," said Michael McDonald, a political science professor at the University of Florida.
 Advertisement Hearst Television's Get the Facts Data Team is tracking early voting across the country using figures from the University of Florida Election Lab, which has tracked early voting since 2008.
 The Get the Facts interactive shows how many early ballots have been received, including in-person and mail ballots, along with available information about voters' party registration and demographic characteristics.
 McDonald says Democrats and voters unaffiliated with a political party are showing strong early participation compared with previous midterm elections, while Republican engagement has been more mixed.
 "Democrats are engaged, and people who aren't affiliated with a political party are engaged. But we're not seeing as high levels of engagement among Republicans," McDonald said in an interview with Hearst Television.
 The differences are particularly striking in North Carolina and several states that traditionally favor Republicans.
 In North Carolina, registered Democrats have cast more than twice as many early ballots as registered Republicans, according to figures from the University of Florida Election Lab.
 McDonald identified another important finding: Registered Republican early participation is below its levels at comparable points in both the 2018 and 2022 midterm elections, even as participation among other groups has increased.
 "Boy, things look really bad for the Republicans in North Carolina," McDonald said.
 President Donald Trump was scheduled to campaign in North Carolina Tuesday night ahead of a competitive Senate race between Republican Michael Whatley and Democrat Roy Cooper.
 McDonald also identified Kansas and Nebraska as states where Democrats are showing surprisingly strong early participation.
 He said registered Democrats are voting at substantially higher levels than registered Republicans in those states at this stage of the election.
 Both states have historically favored Republicans in statewide elections, making the early participation patterns particularly noteworthy.
 In Iowa and Maine, McDonald said Republicans are performing relatively better than in Kansas and Nebraska, although Democrats are also showing strong early participation in those states.
 The differences, he said, broadly reflect the competitive Senate landscape and where political parties are concentrating campaign resources.
 Another surprise involves Black and Latino voters, who McDonald says are showing significantly higher early participation compared with previous elections.
 "So we're seeing numbers that are more than three or four times the level of early voting for Latinos in the data that I'm tracking in North Carolina and Georgia," McDonald said.
 He also found that white voters in North Carolina are participating in early voting at lower levels than at comparable points in the previous two midterm elections, even as Black and Latino participation has increased.
 But McDonald cautions that Republicans could still make up ground closer to Election Day.
 "And it may be that we'll see Republicans start showing up closer to Election Day. In fact, we know that election day tends to be a very red day in terms of the election," McDonald said.
 The University of Florida's data tracks ballots received, not votes for individual candidates. Party registration does not reveal which candidate a voter supported.
 The data also has limitations. Not every state allows or has started early voting, and states differ in what information they report. Changes in voting schedules and election rules can also make historical comparisons difficult.
 That means an apparent advantage in early voting doesn't necessarily translate into an advantage on Election Day.
 The stakes are particularly high in the battle for the U.S. Senate, where Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control. Major battlegrounds include North Carolina, Maine, Ohio and Alaska. Republicans are also defending competitive seats in Iowa, Texas and Kansas, while Democrats are trying to hold key seats in Georgia and Michigan.
 With two weeks until Election Day, both parties are working to turn early participation into votes as the fight for control of Congress enters its final stretch.
